claim:01-erdos-renyi-random-growth.proposition: Random growth produces a homogeneous, hub-free network (Poisson-like degrees) — the null baseline the structured rules are read against.
claim:01-erdos-renyi-random-growth.hypothesis: Random attachment yields a homogeneous Poisson degree distribution with no hubs — the null baseline for every structured rule that follows.

claim:02-preferential-attachment.proposition: Degree-proportional attachment produces scale-free hubs with a power-law degree tail — unlike random growth.
claim:02-preferential-attachment.hypothesis: Linking new nodes preferentially to high-degree nodes yields a power-law degree distribution with a few dominant hubs.

claim:03-small-world-rewiring.proposition: Random rewiring of a ring lattice preserves edge count while shortcuts collapse path length — producing the small-world regime.
claim:03-small-world-rewiring.hypothesis: Rewiring a small fraction of lattice edges collapses path length while clustering stays high — the small-world regime — without changing node or edge counts.

claim:04-fitness-condensation.proposition: Fitness-weighted attachment still builds hubs, but a high-fitness latecomer can overtake older nodes — unlike pure Barabási–Albert.
claim:04-fitness-condensation.hypothesis: Weighting attachment by fitness×degree still produces hubs, but the leading hub need not be the oldest node — fitness breaks the pure first-mover advantage.

claim:05-duplication-divergence.proposition: Copy-then-diverge growth reproduces the heavy-tailed, locally clustered topology seen in protein-interaction networks.
claim:05-duplication-divergence.hypothesis: Copying a random node's neighbourhood and pruning edges yields a heavy-tailed, locally clustered network like observed protein-interaction graphs.

claim:06-forest-fire-densification.proposition: Forest-fire growth densifies the network: mean degree rises as the graph grows, reproducing the densification law.
claim:06-forest-fire-densification.hypothesis: Because each arrival can ignite many links, the edge count grows super-linearly in the node count — the network densifies and its mean degree rises.

claim:07-adaptive-coevolution.proposition: Coevolving opinions and rewiring self-organise the network into like-minded clusters — topology and state adapt to each other.
claim:07-adaptive-coevolution.hypothesis: Letting nodes rewire away from differing neighbours and toward similar ones (while opinions also spread) raises assortativity and segregates the two opinions — the coevolution bridge between Family A and dynamics-on-networks.

claim:08-activity-driven-temporal.proposition: Activity-driven firing produces a sparse, blinking temporal network — each snapshot is instantaneous, unlike the accreting Family-A graphs.
claim:08-activity-driven-temporal.hypothesis: With edges reset every step and nodes firing in proportion to their activity, each instantaneous graph is sparse and blinking, while the time-integrated degree follows the activity distribution.

claim:09-sbml-nodes-coupled.proposition: With an SBML Repressilator at each node and protein diffusion along the edges, the coupled oscillators synchronise — across-node concentration spread collapses.
claim:09-sbml-nodes-coupled.hypothesis: Diffusive coupling of per-node Repressilators pulls their phases together, so the across-node spread of a protein collapses toward zero — synchronisation.

claim:10-sbml-nodes-uncoupled.proposition: With diffusion off, the per-node oscillators remain independent and out of phase — the control that isolates coupling as the cause of synchronisation in study 09.
claim:10-sbml-nodes-uncoupled.hypothesis: Without inter-node transport each Repressilator runs independently, so nodes seeded at different phases never synchronise and the across-node spread stays large.

claim:11-coevolving-growing-network.proposition: Continuous SBML dynamics run correctly on a network being built node-by-node by a PBG reaction: the system stays bounded and oscillating, and most newcomers entrain through the dense local coupling — but synchronisability is topology-dependent, with weakly-attached (low-degree) nodes lagging the synchronised core.
claim:11-coevolving-growing-network.hypothesis: Running the Family-B reactors + transport on a graph that a Family-A growth reaction is simultaneously building, each newcomer joins at its own phase and is pulled into synchrony by the dense local coupling — the full synthesis of dynamics OF and ON the network.

claim:12-coevolving-rewiring-network.proposition: Coupled SBML oscillators synchronise and stay synchronised even as the coupling edges are continuously rewired — reaction–diffusion is robust to an evolving (but well-connected) topology.
claim:12-coevolving-rewiring-network.hypothesis: With the topology continuously small-world-rewired under the running reactors (node and edge counts conserved), the coupling remains strong enough to reach and hold synchrony.

claim:13-quorum-sensing-coupling.hypothesis: A dedicated autoinducer species produced and sensed per node, diffusing along the edges, provides indirect coupling sufficient for synchronisation at lower transport flux than direct protein diffusion.

claim:14-brusselator-model-agnostic.hypothesis: Because NetworkSBMLReactors loads any SBML model and NetworkTransport diffuses any species, pointing them at a Brusselator yields Turing-like patterning / synchronisation on the network with the identical process code.

claim:15-sbml-adaptive-coevolution.hypothesis: Letting each node rewire toward neighbours with a similar SBML observable (e.g. oscillator phase) closes the state→topology feedback and self-organises the network into phase-coherent modules.

narrative.question: How do different local rules reshape a network over time, and can a single process-bigraph process — driven by pluggable reactions — reproduce the canonical families of network dynamics, each with a clear visualization of the network evolving?

units.proposition: Random growth produces a homogeneous, hub-free network (Poisson-like degrees) — the null baseline the structured rules are read against.
Degree-proportional attachment produces scale-free hubs with a power-law degree tail — unlike random growth.
Random rewiring of a ring lattice preserves edge count while shortcuts collapse path length — producing the small-world regime.
Fitness-weighted attachment still builds hubs, but a high-fitness latecomer can overtake older nodes — unlike pure Barabási–Albert.
Copy-then-diverge growth reproduces the heavy-tailed, locally clustered topology seen in protein-interaction networks.
Forest-fire growth densifies the network: mean degree rises as the graph grows, reproducing the densification law.
Coevolving opinions and rewiring self-organise the network into like-minded clusters — topology and state adapt to each other.
Activity-driven firing produces a sparse, blinking temporal network — each snapshot is instantaneous, unlike the accreting Family-A graphs.
With an SBML Repressilator at each node and protein diffusion along the edges, the coupled oscillators synchronise — across-node concentration spread collapses.
With diffusion off, the per-node oscillators remain independent and out of phase — the control that isolates coupling as the cause of synchronisation in study 09.

Continuous SBML dynamics run correctly on a network being built node-by-node by a PBG reaction: the system stays bounded and oscillating, and most newcomers entrain through the dense local coupling — but synchronisability is topology-dependent, with weakly-attached (low-degree) nodes lagging the synchronised core.
Coupled SBML oscillators synchronise and stay synchronised even as the coupling edges are continuously rewired — reaction–diffusion is robust to an evolving (but well-connected) topology.

decisions.detail: Families A/B/C are complete and green (12 studies). Three proposed studies — quorum-sensing coupling, a model-agnostic Brusselator swap, and SBML-state-driven adaptive coevolution — are scoped (status: planned, seeded from studies 09/11/07) as the next extensions.
